def longest_unique(text):
    last = {}
    start = 0
    best_start = 0
    best_len = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(text):
        prev = last.get(ch)
        if prev is not None and prev >= start:
            start = prev + 1
        last[ch] = i
        length = i - start + 1
        if length > best_len:
            best_len = length
            best_start = start
    return text[best_start:best_start+best_len]

Done. `window.py` now uses a single-pass sliding window with a `code point -> last index` map: O(n) time and space instead of the old O(n^2) substring enumeration with per-substring `set()` construction (effectively O(n^3)).

The window only restarts a candidate when a duplicate's previous index falls at or after the current `start`, and `best` is updated only on strictly longer windows, so the earliest substring is preserved on ties.

Verified:
- `test_public.py` -> `PUBLIC_OK`
- 3000 randomized cases (empty, repeated, accented and astral/non-BMP code points) matched a brute-force earliest-longest reference
- explicit tie/case checks (`abcabcbb`, `pwwkew`, `dvdf`, emoji, etc.) all pass
- 500,000-char random input: 0.036s; 200,000 all-distinct code points: 0.042s

Working tree contains only the `window.py` modification.
